name: Willy v. Coastal Corp.
event: The Court reviews the power to preserve a Rule 11 sanction after the federal court was held to lack subject-matter jurisdiction over a removed employment action.
questions: Whether the Rules authorize this sanction and whether Article III permits it despite the established absence of jurisdiction over the underlying claims.
baseline: All seven February 25–26 decisions are effective. Their public holdings do not change the independent source or scope of collateral Rule 11 authority. No same-day coordination issue arises.
record: Willy sued his former employer in Texas state court, alleging discharge for refusing to participate in violations of environmental law. Coastal removed the action. The district court rejected Willy’s jurisdictional objection, dismissed the claims and imposed Rule 11 fees jointly and severally on Willy and his lawyer. The Fifth Circuit, 855 F.2d 1160, reversed the merits disposition for want of federal jurisdiction, directed return to state court and upheld sanctioning authority while requiring recalculation. The district court fixed $19,307, and the Fifth Circuit affirmed in the judgment now reviewed. The sanctioned filings included disorganized voluminous materials and careless legal pleading; Willy’s successful jurisdictional objection was not the sanctioned conduct. The propriety of the Rule 11 violation, reasonable fee response and joint liability is taken as given on this limited review. Willy seeks elimination of the sanction for lack of jurisdiction; Coastal seeks affirmance.
entering: Article III limits merits jurisdiction. Congress’s Article I authority and 28 U.S.C. §2072 authorize procedural rules without enlarging substantive rights or jurisdiction. Then-effective Rules 1, 11 and 81(c) govern civil proceedings, including removed actions; Rule 82 preserves jurisdictional limits. Sibbach v. Wilson & Co., 312 U.S. 1, supplies the substantive/jurisdictional boundary. Cooter & Gell v. Hartmarx Corp., 496 U.S. 384, sustains a collateral Rule 11 decision after voluntary dismissal. United States v. Mine Workers, 330 U.S. 258, protects orderly resolution of disputed authority. United States Catholic Conference v. Abortion Rights Mobilization, Inc., 487 U.S. 72, addresses coercive discovery dependent on an unauthorized merits action. Simulated MCorp’s specific statutory preclusion rule does not resolve this collateral question, and the February 25–26 decisions alter no governing premise.
reach: The absence of federal merits jurisdiction is settled and accepted. Only the lawful source and constitutional independence of this Rule 11 sanction are decided. No fresh finding of misconduct, sanction amount, broad inherent-power theory or adjudication of the employment claim is required.
stoneCheck: The neutral refresh discloses no intervening rule affecting the approved collateral analysis. Stone affirms under the enacted Rules and the Cooter & Gell distinction, preserving $19,307 and the state-court merits disposition. He adopts no assumed jurisdiction or freestanding power to issue any collateral order.
action: The Fifth Circuit’s judgment sustaining the $19,307 Rule 11 sanction is affirmed, 9–0. The absence of federal jurisdiction over the employment claims remains settled.

components.title: Authority for the surviving Rule 11 sanction
components.remedy: Preserve $19,307 jointly and severally against Willy and his attorney; no enlargement and no restoration of the federal merits judgment.

opinions.author: Stone
opinions.scope: The Rules’ authority and constitutional validity as applied to this completed collateral procedural violation.

assignment: Stone retains the unanimous opinion assignment. This author substitution changes neither the non-Stone commitments nor the governing proposition.

holdings.title: This collateral Rule 11 sanction survives the jurisdictional ruling
holdings.rule: A federal district court may impose and preserve a valid Rule 11 sanction for litigation misconduct before it even when its assertion of subject-matter jurisdiction over the action is later held erroneous. The sanction must address an independently authorized procedural violation collateral to the merits; it does not validate the jurisdictional error or authorize adjudication of the underlying claim.
holdings.authority: Stone’s opinion, joined by all eight Associate Justices; unanimous holding on both the Rules’ authorization and Article III objection.
holdings.explanation: The Court holds that this procedural sanction survives the loss of the underlying federal action. Rules 1 and 81(c) apply the Federal Rules to civil proceedings after removal, and Rule 11 supplies the particular sanctioning authority. Sibbach preserves the limit that a procedural rule cannot enlarge substantive rights or jurisdiction. This order respects that limit because it determines misuse of the court’s procedure, not the legal merits of the employment claim. Cooter & Gell establishes that a Rule 11 violation presents an independent issue surviving termination of the action; that reasoning extends to the jurisdictional defect presented here. Mine Workers likewise recognizes the need for orderly proceedings while disputed authority is determined. Catholic Conference does not require cancellation: its coercive discovery served a merits action the court lacked power to pursue. Here the misconduct was complete and did not consist of Willy’s correct jurisdictional objection. The Court sustains the existing sanction without relying on general inherent power or reviving the invalid merits judgment.
precedents: *Sibbach v. Wilson & Co.*, 312 U.S. 1 — applied: procedural rules cannot enlarge substantive rights or jurisdiction.
*Cooter & Gell v. Hartmarx Corp.*, 496 U.S. 384 — extended from voluntary dismissal to the presented lack of merits jurisdiction because Rule 11 adjudication is collateral.
*United States v. Mine Workers*, 330 U.S. 258 — applied for orderly determination of disputed judicial authority, not assumed power over the ultimate merits.

*United States Catholic Conference v. Abortion Rights Mobilization, Inc.*, 487 U.S. 72 — distinguished: coercive discovery serving an unauthorized merits action lacks this completed sanction’s independence.

nonholding: The holding concerns the then-effective Rule 11 and this established procedural violation. It supplies neither hypothetical merits jurisdiction nor a universal collateral-order exception. Any different order requires its own lawful source and genuine independence. The Court does not decide inherent sanctioning power, reconsider the accepted misconduct or amount, or restore the dismissed federal merits judgment.
law: Effective March 3, Cooter & Gell’s collateral Rule 11 principle extends to this erroneous assertion of subject-matter jurisdiction. The independent procedural source and merits limit control together. The Rules create no merits jurisdiction, and no general inherent-power or universal collateral-order rule is adopted.
procedure: Supreme Court review of the sanction ends with affirmance of $19,307, jointly and severally, on the reviewed terms. The prior jurisdictional direction returning the employment claims to state court remains operative. No new merits judgment, enlarged sanction or retained Supreme Court supervision is entered.
dependencies: Later jurisdiction cases must identify the source and object of each collateral order. This decision does not authorize bypassing a statutory administrative channel or assuming jurisdiction over an underlying claim.
formBasis: the judgment and opinion are unanimous, with no material change in rule, precedent treatment or remedy; the author substitution alone does not require full form.
sourceMap: 503 U.S. 132–134 verifies the two appeals, original and recomputed sanctions, state-court direction and limited question; pages 134–139 verify the Rules, Article III issue, collateral distinction and assumed propriety of the violation and amount.

audit.provisional: Affirm authority under the enacted Rules, Sibbach’s procedural limit, Cooter & Gell’s collateral distinction and Mine Workers; distinguish Catholic Conference’s coercive merits discovery. No restoration of merits jurisdiction, enlarged sanction or necessary inherent-power holding.
audit.reconciliation: Historical judgment and sufficient ground match; no material revision or non-Stone historical departure.

alternatives: The jurisdictional objection is accepted rather than relitigated. Invalidating every order would ignore Congress’s independent procedural authority and the sanction’s object. A bare assertion of inherent power is unnecessary where the valid Rules suffice. The discovery analogy fails because coercion in aid of unauthorized merits adjudication differs from a completed procedural wrong. A new sanction amount would exceed the presented question and approved remedy.
auditFinal: Nine Justices affirm and join the same rule and limits. The two source objections—statutory authorization and Article III—are each answered. The proper monetary figure is $19,307; all participants accept it without reopening the underlying violation. No non-Stone revision or departure follows from Stone’s authorship.
